en: The Sūtra on the Five Dharmas of a Bhikṣu Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee and Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Great Master for Transmitting the Teachings, Subject Fata, in accordance with the Imperial Decree.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling there for the sake of observing the future.

At that time, immeasurable devas and humans, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was the Teacher of gods and men, venerated, made offerings to, honored, and praised him with reverence and faith; they attained the highest benefit, happiness, renown, and fame, each presenting him with renowned robes, exquisite food, bedding, and medicinal decoctions.
At that time, for the sake of their benefit and happiness, the World-Honored One accepted and made use of everything without any defilement or attachment, like a lotus in water.

He did so only to enable the multitudes of sentient beings among gods and humans to obtain the fruits of supreme merit and attain wondrous adornment; he bestowed ambrosia upon those gods and humans, causing them to dwell in reliance [upon the Dharma] for a long, long time.

Furthermore, they cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings to obtain the nectar of immortality, even leading them across the sufferings of saṃsāra—birth, old age, sickness, and death—and even liberating them from the great perils of the hells, so that they may attain peace, tranquility, and equanimity, being free from fear and dread, and attaining nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, without departing from the kingdoms of Magadha, Vṛji-maṇḍala, Kāśī, Kośala, and Kurupañcāla, kings such as Vañca, Maccha, Śūrasena, Śibi, and Naśarāṇava—upon seeing [the Buddha], all these kings were subdued by the power of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Furthermore, they are able to walk upon the celestial walking paths, the Brahma walking paths, the Śakra walking paths, the empty walking paths, the tranquil walking paths, the walking paths of the Buddhas, the walking paths of the Teachers, the walking paths of the Knowers, and the walking paths of the Perfectly Awakened Ones; thereby attaining the opening and liberation of the mind and achieving the supreme *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, Blessed One, regarding all places for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) and whatever walking meditation one seeks to perform, one is able to practice them all.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"There are five qualities that should be fully maintained; these are the practices that bhikṣus of the future should constantly carry out."
What are the five factors?

This bhikṣu does not know what constitutes an āpatti, nor what does not constitute an āpatti; he does not know what constitutes a light āpatti, nor what constitutes a heavy āpatti; and he is newly ordained, having fewer than five years of seniority.
"O Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu is endowed with these five qualities, that bhikṣu is not fit to dwell in the practice of exhortation.
O Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu is known to be endowed with these five qualities, that bhikṣu is fit to dwell in the practice of exhortation."
What are the five dharmas?

This bhikṣu knows what constitutes an āpatti, knows what does not constitute an āpatti, knows light āpattis, and knows heavy āpattis; he has completed five years [of standing] or has more than five years remaining.
"O Bhikṣus, one who is fully endowed with these five qualities may remain as a bhikṣu who encourages others in their duties.
Furthermore, there are five other qualities; if a bhikṣu is fully endowed with these, he must not live apart from his preceptor."

What are the five qualities? This bhikṣu does not know the Prātimokṣa; he does not know how to recite the Prātimokṣa; he does not know the delimitation of boundaries; he does not know the matters concerning the delimitation of boundaries; and he is a newly ordained monk who has been less than five years ordained.
If a bhikṣu possesses these five qualities, he must not live apart from his preceptor.
If a bhikṣu is fully endowed with these five qualities, that bhikṣu may live apart from his preceptor.
What are the five qualities?

This bhikṣu knows the Prātimokṣa of the bhikṣus, knows how to recite the Prātimokṣa, knows the delimitation of boundaries, knows the procedure for delimiting boundaries, and has completed five years or more than five years [of seniority].
"Monks, when a bhikṣu is endowed with these five qualities, he may dwell independently without relying on a preceptor.
Monks, there are another five qualities; when a bhikṣu is endowed with these, he must not dwell independently without relying on a preceptor."
What are the five factors?

This bhikṣu does not know the *poṣadha*, he does not know the duties of the *poṣadha*, he does not know the ritual for establishing the boundary (*sīmā*), he does not know the duties of establishing the boundary, and he is a newly ordained monk who has been less than five years.
“Bhikṣus, if one is endowed with these five qualities, one must not dwell apart from one’s preceptor.
Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu is endowed with these five qualities, that bhikṣu may dwell apart from his preceptor.”
What are the five dharmas?
This bhikṣu knows the *poṣadha* of the bhikṣus, knows the duties of the *poṣadha*, knows the boundary, knows the duties of the boundary, and has completed five years—or more than five years.
“Monks, when a bhikṣu is endowed with these five qualities, he attains dwelling free from dependence.
Furthermore, monks, there are five right mindfulnesses.
What are the five right mindfulnesses?”
That is to say: conduct, retribution, response, life, and at the end of life, one does not think of worldly gain but of transcending the world.
Bhikṣus! These are the five right mindfulnesses.
"Furthermore, monks,
there are five other bases for right mindfulness.
What are these five?
That is to say: food and drink, ritual services, not overstepping the teacher’s boundary, dwelling together with the teacher, and the five-year period of clear discernment.
These are the five bases of mindfulness. "O Bhikṣus!"
One should know that these five—namely, reliance, right mindfulness, retribution, and so forth—are *āpatti*.
What kind of *āpatti* should one know?
One should know the five types of *āpatti*.
What are these five?
They are the *pārājika*, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the *pāyattika* precepts; it should be known that each of these is explained in four ways, while the fifth is the *ajñāpanna*.
Thus one knows what is *āpatti*.
Furthermore, one knows what is not *āpatti*.
How does one know the characteristics of what is not *āpatti*?
One constantly practices what is not an *āpatti*, and thus knows what is not an *āpatti*.
Furthermore, one knows light *āpattis*.
How does one know light *āpattis*?
This refers to practicing deep fear regarding the minor *āpatti* offenses. How does one practice?

It means practicing the minor *āpatti* offenses concerning the four *pārājika* dharmas; practicing the minor *āpatti* offenses concerning the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas; practicing the minor *āpatti* offenses concerning the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas; practicing the minor *āpatti* offenses concerning the ninety-two *pāyattika* dharmas; and practicing the purification of the ninety-two *pāyattika* dharmas by reciting each of the four [confessions] as minor *āpatti* offenses, along with the minor *āpatti* offenses concerning the remaining fifty rules of training.
If one acts in such a manner, one incurs a light *āpatti*.
Thus one knows the light *āpatti*;
next, one knows the heavy *āpatti*.
How does one know the gravity of the *āpatti*?

Regarding the conduct that incurs a grave *āpatti*, and the remaining conduct of the fifty rules of the *dharma* that constitute grave *āpatti*, each is declared four times; the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules constitute grave *āpatti* through the purity of one's conduct;
the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules are purified, and the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules constitute grave *āpatti* through the purity of one's conduct.
The thirty *pāyattika* rules of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) are purified; the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are purified by means of the formal procedure of *praty-āpatti*;
the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are purified; and the four *pārājika* rules are purified by means of the formal procedure of *praty-āpatti*.
When one has performed such conduct, one incurs a *guru-apatti*.
Thus one recognizes a *guru-apatti*.
This is five years, this is a full five years, this is more than five years; in this way, one obtains reliance through faith (*śraddhā-niśraya*).
"Furthermore, there is the knowledge of the Prātimokṣa. How does one know the Prātimokṣa? One knows: 'This is the Prātimokṣa';

one contemplates and observes it while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; one observes the past, present, and future manifestations of body, speech, and mind, and examines these sublime conducts. In this way, one knows the Prātimokṣa."
Next, one should know the exposition of the Prātimokṣa.
How does one know the exposition of the Prātimokṣa? There are seven Prātimokṣas.
What are the seven?
How should they be explained?
One explains the four *pārājika* dharmas; the rest is as has been heard.
When this first recitation of the Prātimokṣa is being spoken,
it is followed by the recitation of the four Pārājika rules and the thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa rules, as well as whatever else has been heard.
When this second recitation of the Prātimokṣa is being delivered,
one should next recite the four Pārājika rules, the thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa rules, and the thirty Naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules, as well as whatever else has been heard.
When this third recitation of the Prātimokṣa is being spoken,

one should next speak of the four pārājika dharmas, the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas, the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika dharmas, and the ninety-two pāyattika dharmas for the sake of purity, as well as whatever else has been heard.
When this fourth recitation of the Prātimokṣa is being spoken,

one should next explain the four Pārājika rules, the thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa rules, the thirty Naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules, and the ninety-two Pāyattika rules for purification, each with its fourfold exposition, as well as whatever else has been heard.

When this fifth recitation of the Prātimokṣa is being delivered, one next recites the four Pārājika rules, the thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa rules, the thirty Naiḥsargika-Pāyattika rules, and the ninety-two Pāyattika rules, etc., for the sake of purity; each of these is recited four times, as are the fifty training rules, along with whatever else has been heard.
When this sixth recitation of the Prātimokṣa has been spoken,
each [rule] shall then be explained in detail;
this is the seventh recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
Thus is the Prātimokṣa spoken; thus is the Prātimokṣa known and spoken. [One] knows the delimitation of the boundary.
"How does one know the delimitation of the boundary?"
This refers to the fact that the present assembly performs the boundary-binding on the fourteenth and fifteenth days;
thus one knows the binding of the boundary.
Next, one knows the matters concerning the binding of the boundary.
How does one know the matters concerning the establishment of a boundary (*sīmā*)?
First, the undertaking; second, the requesting of names; third, the request; fourth, the request for the fivefold assembly to establish the boundary.
In this way, one knows the matters concerning the establishment of a boundary.
"It is five years; it is exactly five years; it is more than five years"—knowing thus, one attains reliance upon mindfulness.
Next, one knows the *poṣadha*.
How does one know the *poṣadha*?
Today is the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the fortnight for the *poṣadha*.
Thus one should know the *poṣadha*;
next, one should know the matters concerning the *poṣadha*.
How does one know the matter of *poṣadha*?
First, undertaking; second, requesting the name; third, requesting; fourth, requesting; fifth, the communal *poṣadha*.
In this way, one knows the *poṣadha*.
Next is the knowledge of boundary-establishment (*sīmābandha*). What is the knowledge of boundary-establishment?
It consists of five kinds.
There are five ways of establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*); thus one should know the matter of establishing the boundary.
How does one know the matter of establishing the boundary?

One who has committed an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) may not establish a boundary; one should sit on a low seat while eating and drinking, and once the food and drink have been prepared, one should perform what is to be done.
In this way, one understands the matter of the boundary:
"This is five years," "This is a full five years," or "This is the remainder of five years.
In this way, one attains mindfulness of dependence.
"Furthermore, there is the practice of the Way.
What is the practice of the Way?
It refers to the practice of the ācārya."
Practicing the path in this manner is the basis for mindfulness.
Next is the analysis of the practice of the path. How is it analyzed?
"Knowing the preceptor’s recitation of the precepts and knowing one's own recitation of the precepts—in this way, one obtains reliance through mindfulness.
Furthermore, there is the distinction of 'past time.
What is meant by 'past time'?"
That is to say, when the preceptor has passed away and one has likewise passed the time [of dependence], one may thus obtain a formal reliance (*niśraya*).
Such passing of time is not for the sake of material gain.
How is it not for the sake of material gain?
That is to say, the ācārya residing in that saṃghārāma does not act for the sake of material gain; thus one obtains the support of mindfulness.
Likewise, he does not travel for half a month for the sake of profit and offerings.
What is the practice of the half-month?
It refers to the preceptor performing communal confession every half-month.
In this way, one obtains the reliance upon mindfulness.
In this way, one practices the *anāpatti* (absence of offense) for half a month.
What is meant by *anāpatti*?
It refers to when an *ācārya* instructs one to go to such-and-such a person to receive dependence (*niśraya*).
In this way, one attains reliance upon mindfulness.
Furthermore, regarding "conduct":
what is meant by conduct?
That is to say, based on the words of the ācārya, "I do not require you to rely upon me for your practice," one thus attains mindfulness as one's reliance;
practicing in this manner, one does not transgress the boundary of the teacher.
What is meant by not transgressing the teacher’s boundary?
It means not transgressing the teacher’s village boundary.
In this way, one obtains the support of mindfulness; thus, one does not transgress the teacher’s village boundary.
Confession before one’s teacher.
What is confession before one’s teacher?
It refers to confessing before one’s teacher every half-month; in this way, one obtains reliance through mindfulness.
"In this way, having clearly practiced repentance under the same teacher for five years, one attains the reliance of mindfulness.
'Monks! You should be fully endowed with these five kinds of dharmas; you should practice according to these rules of the bhikṣu.'"
"In that Dharma there is no *āpatti*; whatever precepts exist therein, one shall obtain *naiḥśreyasa* day by day.
When the World-Honored One had thus spoken these five dharmas, the assembly of bhikṣus, as well as the humans and devas, paid homage, circumambulated him, and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Five Dharmas of a Bhikṣu Spoken by the Buddha
